name: Meningitis
definition: Meningitis is an infection of the protective membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.
overview: The NHS says meningitis is usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection, and fungi can also be a cause. Viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious, while bacterial meningitis is the more serious form and needs treatment in hospital. Symptoms can develop suddenly. The NHS gives the same emergency advice for meningitis and sepsis: call 999 or go to A&E. Vaccination is the main way of preventing some bacterial causes.
causes: A viral or bacterial infection is the usual cause.
Fungi can also cause meningitis, and fungal cases develop more slowly.
Viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious.
Bacterial meningitis is the more serious form.
The infections spread through close contact with someone who carries the infection.
riskFactors: Prolonged close contact with a person who has meningococcal disease in a household-type setting in the days before their illness began.
UKHSA lists household members, partners and university students who share a kitchen as examples of close contacts.
signs: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is a key warning sign, though not everyone with meningitis has one.
In babies, a bulging soft spot on the top of the head.
Early signs of sepsis alongside suspected meningococcal disease.
Meningococcal disease may be missed in older adults who have delirium or altered consciousness.
complications: Problems with movement, balance and coordination.
Loss of digits or limbs in some people.
diagnosis: The doctor examines the person, asks about symptoms and may arrange blood tests and a lumbar puncture, which collects a sample of cerebrospinal fluid for examination. A CT scan may be used to look for brain problems such as swelling. When bacterial infection is suspected, antibiotics usually start before the diagnosis is confirmed, and the WHO says a lumbar puncture should never delay them.
treatment: Treatment depends on whether the cause is viral or bacterial. Bacterial meningitis is treated in hospital, usually for at least a week, with antibiotics and fluids given into a vein and oxygen through a face mask if needed. Steroid medicine is sometimes added to reduce swelling around the brain. Viral meningitis usually improves on its own within 7 to 10 days and can often be managed at home with rest, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine. Fungal meningitis is treated with antifungal medicine.
prevention: The NHS describes vaccination as the main way to prevent some causes of meningitis, with MenB for babies, MenACWY for teenagers and the 6-in-1, pneumococcal and MMRV vaccines in the routine schedule. Close contacts of someone with meningococcal disease are offered antibiotics to clear the bacteria from the nose.
seekCare: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to the nearest A&E immediately if meningitis or sepsis is suspected, and says that waiting for every symptom or for a rash is not advised. NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear whether symptoms are serious. UKHSA guidance says close contacts who become unwell should seek urgent medical attention even if they took preventive antibiotics.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of meningitis?
sections.body:
The NHS says meningitis symptoms can develop suddenly. They include a high temperature, very cold hands and feet, a stiff neck, joint and muscle pain, a severe headache that keeps getting worse, and seizures. A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is a key warning sign, but not everyone with meningitis develops spots or a rash.

Babies and young children can show different signs, such as refusing feeds, being irritable, having a high-pitched cry or having a bulging soft spot on the top of the head. The WHO notes that symptoms can differ depending on the cause and how quickly the illness progresses, and that serious complications such as sepsis can occur. Several NHS pages say that the full set of symptoms, or a rash, should not be waited for.

The NICE guideline lists a rash that does not fade under pressure and early signs of sepsis as features that should raise suspicion of meningococcal disease. It also notes that the disease may be missed in older adults who have delirium or altered consciousness.

sections.heading: What causes meningitis and how does it spread?
sections.body:
The NHS says meningitis is usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection. Viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious, while bacterial meningitis is the more serious form. Meningitis Research Foundation material adds that fungi can also cause it, and that fungal cases develop more slowly and are treated with antifungal medicine.

The infections that cause meningitis spread through close contact with someone who carries the infection. UKHSA guidance on meningococcal disease defines a close contact as a person who had prolonged close contact with the case in a household-type setting in the 7 days before the illness began. Examples it gives include household members, partners and university students who share a kitchen.

UKHSA describes the signs of meningococcal disease as meningitis and sepsis, which is why the two are often named together in public health advice.

sections.heading: How is meningitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
NHS material says the doctor examines the person, asks about symptoms and may arrange blood tests and a lumbar puncture. A lumbar puncture collects a sample of cerebrospinal fluid so that it can be examined. A CT scan may be used to look for brain problems such as swelling.

When a bacterial cause is suspected, antibiotics usually start before the diagnosis is confirmed and are stopped later if tests show a viral cause. The WHO stresses that a lumbar puncture should never delay antibiotics when bacterial infection is suspected.

For suspected meningococcal disease, NICE recommends a bacterial throat swab for meningococcal culture, preferably taken before antibiotics. It says that tests in hospital are usually done before antibiotics are given, although antibiotics may need to start before the results are available.

sections.heading: How is meningitis treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on whether the cause is viral or bacterial. Bacterial meningitis needs hospital treatment, usually for at least a week. Hospital care includes antibiotics and fluids given into a vein, and oxygen through a face mask if needed. Steroid medicine is sometimes added to reduce swelling around the brain, and the WHO recommends giving it with the first antibiotic dose in non-epidemic settings.

NICE recommends that antibiotics for suspected meningococcal disease start within 1 hour of arrival at hospital, and that they are given before hospital arrival when the disease is strongly suspected. UKHSA guidance gives rapid admission to hospital as the highest priority when meningococcal disease is suspected.

Viral meningitis usually improves on its own within 7 to 10 days. It can often be managed at home with rest, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine.

sections.heading: Can meningitis be prevented?
sections.body:
The NHS describes vaccination as the main way of preventing meningitis caused by several bacteria. The routine schedule includes the MenB vaccine for babies, the MenACWY vaccine for teenagers, and the 6-in-1, pneumococcal and MMRV vaccines. UKHSA says vaccines reduce the risk of becoming severely ill, being admitted to hospital and developing long-term complications.

People who have been in close contact with someone who has meningococcal disease are offered antibiotics to clear the bacteria from the nose. UKHSA guidance says these are ideally started within 24 hours of the first person's diagnosis. It says close contacts can attend school or work as normal unless they become unwell, and it does not advise face masks in education settings to prevent spread.

The guidance adds that contacts who become unwell should seek urgent medical attention, even if they have taken the preventive antibiotics.

sections.heading: What are the after-effects and how does recovery go?
sections.body:
Most people recover from meningitis, but the after-effects depend on the cause. Viral meningitis does not usually cause long-term problems, although headaches, exhaustion and memory loss can follow and, for some people, last a long time. Very rarely, cognitive or neurological problems persist.

Bacterial meningitis can cause lasting harm. Possible after-effects include hearing or vision loss, seizures, movement and coordination problems, and difficulty with memory and concentration. Some people lose digits or limbs. Meningitis Research Foundation material reports that around one in five people who have bacterial meningitis are left with permanent after-effects.

Support can include rehabilitation, prosthetic limbs where limbs were amputated, and counselling if the experience causes problems such as disturbed sleep or fear of doctors and hospitals. Charities such as Meningitis Research Foundation and Meningitis Now offer information and support.

faqs.q: How are meningitis and sepsis linked?
faqs.a: The NHS gives the same emergency advice for both: call 999 or go to A&E immediately if either is suspected. NICE lists early signs of sepsis among the features that should raise suspicion of meningococcal disease, and UKHSA describes the signs of meningococcal disease as meningitis and sepsis. The WHO notes that sepsis is among the serious complications that can affect how meningitis shows itself.

faqs.q: What is the difference between viral and bacterial meningitis?
faqs.a: The NHS says viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious, while bacterial meningitis is more serious. Bacterial meningitis needs hospital treatment, usually for at least a week, with antibiotics into a vein. Viral meningitis usually improves on its own within 7 to 10 days and can often be managed at home.

faqs.q: Does everyone with meningitis get a rash?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is a key warning sign, but not everyone with meningitis gets spots or a rash. Several NHS pages say that people should not wait for a rash, or for every symptom, to appear before getting urgent help by calling 999 or going to A&E.

The NHS says the infections that cause meningitis spread through close contact with someone who carries the infection. Close contacts of a person with meningococcal disease are offered antibiotics. UKHSA says they can usually attend school or work as normal, unless they become unwell, when they should seek urgent medical advice.

faqs.q: Do people fully recover from meningitis?
faqs.a: Most people recover, but it depends on the cause. Viral meningitis does not usually cause long-term problems. Bacterial meningitis can leave lasting effects such as hearing loss, vision loss, seizures or memory and concentration problems. Meningitis Research Foundation says most children who have bacterial meningitis or meningococcal sepsis survive without permanent after-effects.
